Never tried them. I pass no moral judgment against those who do though. And they certainly appear to open some creative doors. Where would the Beatles be without LSD?

The problem I have with them personally stems from fear, particularly the fear of nor being in control or the fear of liking them too much. Syd Barrett, formerly of Pink Floyd, is a case study in the consequences of abusing LSD. And John Lennon was dropping on a near daily basis to the point that he became a total asshole.

particularly the fear of nor being in control or the fear of liking them too much

It's pretty challenging to abuse psychedelics. There's no physical addiction, so you don't get the 'I feel like shit right now because my body is demanding more' situation. They're insanely exhausting to use, and people who abuse them are generally abusing some kind of upper (to re-energize them) or downer (so they don't feel how tired they really are) as well. Psychedelic abuse (particularly LSD abuse) mainly only happens to people with access to a ridiculously large supply. When you start viewing a tab as worth $2 instead of $10, $15, or even $20, it gets a lot easier to take way more than you need to just because you can.

But yeah, the fear of losing control over one's consciousness is one of the leading causes of bad trips. People can't let go and just let it happen, so it becomes a walking on hot coals scenario; running across actually makes it worse.

I've never had a bad LSD experience, save for a few minutes after a gigantic wolf spider scared the shit out of me. Mushrooms pretty much always make me sick to my stomach... People say that the feeling goes away after you throw up, but I'm not a big fan of any activity where vomiting is a requirement. The one time they didn't make me sick, it was like a more-emotional, less-intellectual version of LSD.

They could definitely have an impact on society if they saw widespread use. They make letting go of negative concepts extremely easy. Lying becomes more difficult, even for a few days afterward. The thought of lying to someone just seems so repulsive that is extremely difficult to do. Money becomes something that allows you to do what you love - the idea of having money just to have money becomes totally ridiculous. Violence and anger become repulsive. It allows you to view the world as if you were seeing it through the eyes of a child once more. Hearing people blurt out deceptively simple-sounding insights is common.

I can honestly say I felt like a more relaxed, more considerate person when I was using psychedelics 'regularly' (about every 6 to 8 weeks). Most of my experiences were with LSD. It's not an addictive substance; using it is physically, mentally, and emotionally exhausting. After coming down from an LSD trip, the last thing on my mind is using LSD again. Do people abuse it? Sure. Every drug has its abusers. But there are no withdrawal symptoms, and barring high blood pressure and psychological damage from a severely bad trip (which is usually caused by irresponsible use of the substance in the first place), it's one of the least-harmful scheduled narcotics. Less harmful than caffeine, even, according to research. Having said that, hang around people who use LSD regularly, and you'll eventually encounter 'that one guy' who abuses it so much that it's like their soul has been melted. Really creepy and really sad. I don't know how else to describe it... It's like their mental, spiritual, and physical selves are no longer 'connected' properly.

In my opinion, LSD is demonized the way it is because it helps people reflect on - and be truly happy with - what they already have. It makes people nonviolent. LSD is illegal because it helps people realize the banality of consumerism and the pointlessness of violence. No consumerism means corporations can't squeeze money out of people by making them feel inadequate. More citizens who actually support nonviolence (not stupid hippies who talk about how it would be easier if we all just loved each other, but people who actually, actively support nonviolence/pacifism) means its more difficult to perpetuate consumption via war.

Do I think it being legal/acceptable/widely used would solve all our problems? Fuck no. Do I think it has the potential to do good? Definitely. Do I think it's something (most) people should try at least once? Yes.

If you're smart, and you do drugs, they can open your mind.

If you're stupid, and you do drugs, you'll end up in prison.
